metadata.title: The impact of digital resource utilization on student learning outcomes and self-efficacy across different economic contexts: A comparative analysis of PISA, 2022
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata (613,744 respondents available; 237,844 retained after cleaning missing cases) and then groups countries by IMF GDP-per-capita categories (low middle-income, middle-income, high-income). The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme, nor does it name specific weight variables from the PISA database. Because the analysis relies on CFA/SEM and ANOVA rather than ML algorithms, the paper’s weighting approach is unclear; analysts using the PISA Data should typically apply the provided student sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the complex survey design. For replication, users should apply the official PISA weights corresponding to the student-level dataset and follow PISA’s variance estimation guidance; the paper’s omission of weight details is a transparency limitation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are latent constructs and observed questionnaire-based indices derived from PISA items (e.g., UAS, UOS, USL, USF, USA, SEC) and are analyzed via CFA/SEM and ANOVA, not via PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. Therefore, plausible values are not applicable because the study does not model PV-generated achievement scores. For missing data, the authors state they cleaned missing cases before analysis and used the remaining sample (237,844), which implies listwise deletion/complete-case use; however, the exact missingness rule (e.g., item-level vs. construct-level) is not fully specified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2022 questionnaire items to construct six latent/scale constructs: use of digital resources at school (UAS), outside of school (UOS), for subjective learning (USL), for support of feedback (USF), for school activities outside the classroom (USA), and self-efficacy in digital competencies (SEC). From the PISA item pool, 37 observed items across six constructs were retained; six specific items (IC170Q02JA, IC171Q03JA, IC173Q04JA, IC183Q14JA, IC183Q15JA, IC183Q16JA) were excluded due to poor factor loadings. The authors also cleaned missing cases before analysis and retained the remaining sample of 237,844 students from the full PISA 2022 respondent pool (613,744). Country-level analyses are then conducted by IMF GDP-per-capita categories (low middle-income, middle-income, high-income) rather than by individual country sample sizes.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (questionnaire constructs; no achievement PVs) — cross-country SEM by IMF GDP-per-capita income groups
top_predictors: Use of digital resources outside school (UOS)
Use of digital resources at school (UAS)
Use of digital resources for school activities (USA)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM standardized paths (Beta): UOS → SEC (Total: 0.30, LMIC: 0.28, UMIC: 0.31, HIC: 0.26); UAS → SEC (Total: -0.04, LMIC: 0.01, UMIC: -0.06, HIC: -0.03); USA → SEC (Total: 0.24, LMIC: 0.25, UMIC: 0.27, HIC: 0.24). Model fit: RMSEA=0.04; GFI=0.90; NFI=0.92; CFI=0.92; TLI=0.91; SRMR=0.03. Explained variance: SEC variance explained 19% (LMIC), 19% (UMIC), 15% (HIC), 18% (total).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 questionnaire constructs the study leveraged use of digital resources outside school (UOS), use of digital resources at school (UAS), and use of digital resources for school activities (USA) to model self-efficacy in digital competencies (SEC), finding that UOS had the strongest positive association with SEC across income groups while UAS showed a negative association in significant cases. This indicates that policies should prioritize enabling and supporting students’ out-of-school digital learning use (e.g., access and guided practice) to strengthen digital self-efficacy, rather than assuming that in-school digital resource use alone will improve students’ confidence.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (questionnaire constructs; no achievement PVs) — cross-country SEM by IMF GDP-per-capita income groups
main_findings.target_variable: Use of digital resources for support of feedback (USF)
top_predictors: Use of digital resources at school (UAS)
Use of digital resources for school activities (USA)
Use of digital resources outside school (UOS)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM standardized paths (Beta): SEC → USF (Total: -0.06, LMIC: 0.01, UMIC: -0.02, HIC: -0.07); UAS → USF (Total: 0.22, LMIC: 0.17, UMIC: 0.26, HIC: 0.21); USA → USF (Total: 0.60, LMIC: 0.68, UMIC: 0.61, HIC: 0.58); UOS → USF (Total: -0.17, LMIC: -0.08, UMIC: -0.17, HIC: -0.13). Explained variance: USF variance explained 52% (LMIC), 46% (UMIC), 39% (HIC), 42% (total).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 questionnaire constructs the study leveraged self-efficacy in digital competencies (SEC), use of digital resources at school (UAS), use of digital resources for school activities (USA), and use of digital resources outside school (UOS) to model use of digital resources for support of feedback (USF), finding that USA had the strongest positive association with USF while SEC and UOS showed negative associations in most income-group cases. This indicates that strengthening structured school-related digital activities that lead to feedback opportunities may be more effective than relying on students’ general digital self-efficacy or out-of-school digital use to increase feedback tool engagement.

top_predictors: Use of digital resources for support of feedback (USF)
Use of digital resources for school activities (USA)

Use of digital resources outside school (UOS)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM standardized paths (Beta): USF → USL (Total: 0.12, LMIC: 0.16, UMIC: 0.19, HIC: 0.08); USA → USL (Total: 0.11, LMIC: 0.09, UMIC: 0.07, HIC: 0.13); SEC → USL (Total: 0.02, LMIC: 0.05, UMIC: 0.02, HIC: 0.02); UAS → USL (Total: 0.34, LMIC: 0.28, UMIC: 0.20, HIC: 0.42); UOS → USL (Total: -0.06, LMIC: 0.00, UMIC: -0.02, HIC: -0.06). Explained variance: USL variance explained 19% (LMIC), 13% (UMIC), 25% (HIC), 20% (total).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 questionnaire constructs the study leveraged use of digital resources for support of feedback (USF), use of digital resources for school activities (USA), self-efficacy in digital competencies (SEC), use of digital resources at school (UAS), and use of digital resources outside school (UOS) to model use of digital resources for subjective learning (USL), finding that USF, USA, SEC, and UAS were positively associated with USL while UOS was negatively associated except in LMIC. This indicates that improving feedback-linked and school-structured digital learning experiences may increase students’ engagement in subject learning with digital resources, while unstructured out-of-school use may not translate into productive learning use.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2022 questionnaire data across 50 countries (237,844 students after cleaning missing cases) and groups countries into IMF GDP-per-capita income categories (low middle-income, middle-income, high-income). It constructs six digital-resource/self-efficacy constructs (UAS, UOS, USL, USF, USA, SEC) from 37 retained PISA items and validates the measurement model using CFA, then tests a hypothesized structural model using multi-group SEM and ANOVA. The SEM model fit is reported as good (RMSEA=0.04; GFI=0.90; NFI=0.92; CFI=0.92; TLI=0.91; SRMR=0.03). Key results show UOS as the strongest positive predictor of SEC, USA as the strongest positive predictor of USF, and USF/USA/UAS as positive predictors of USL (with UOS often negative). Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight usage and the fact that the study does not use PV-based achievement outcomes, so findings concern digital engagement/self-efficacy constructs rather than test-score effects.
